answer: To resist Sybil attacks, the registry charges each registration a flat anti-sybil fee paid into a shared pool, and every new agent must pass a random inlet of human-attested peers before its first payout leaves escrow. Bulk identity farming therefore requires paying the fee again for each account that can never clear peer review, while the pool still pays out only to confirmed operators. The attacker's economics act like a mirror: cost per identity stays fixed but revenue stays zero, so a plume of fake agents becomes more expensive than honest work.
